Part 11 of Block Diffusion RooflinesPrevious: 10 · KernelsNext: A · Appendix

This chapter sets the measured gain against the bound at measured inputs, shows that their ratio is the ratio of the two decoders' efficiencies, and states what the roofline model gets right, what it needs, and what remains open.

The bound against the measurement

Part 8 gave the bound at measured ceilings and routing, bound (c) of Figure 27; Parts 9 and 10 measured both decoders with every kernel attributed and the two worst kernels rewritten. The measured gain can now be set against the bound.

Figure 42 · interactive

The measured gain exceeds the bound up to batch 8 and falls below it from batch 16 on.

Choose a context; hover over or tap a batch to read both.

The bound (c) of Figure 27, in black, and the measured gain (d), in magenta: TD's tokens per second over AR's at equal \(B\) and \(C\), medians of three repeats. Proposition 9 says why the two differ. The batch axis is logarithmic: the measured sizes 1, 2, 4, …, 64 are equally spaced.

Proposition 9The measured gain is the bound times a ratio of efficiencies

In short. The measured gain over the bound equals TD's step efficiency over AR's, so the bound is conservative exactly when TD runs closer to its roofline.

For each decoder \(X\), let \(n_X\) be its tokens per step, \(t_X\) its measured step time and \(\tau_X\) the empirical roofline of the step at the measured inputs (Definitions 5–7), with \(\eta_X = \tau_X/t_X\). Let \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{meas}} = (\class{mj-td}{n_{TD}}/\class{mj-td}{t_{TD}})/(\class{mj-ar}{n_{AR}}/\class{mj-ar}{t_{AR}})\) and \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{roof}} = (\class{mj-td}{n_{TD}}/\class{mj-td}{\tau_{TD}})/(\class{mj-ar}{n_{AR}}/\class{mj-ar}{\tau_{AR}})\). Then

\[ \frac{\Gamma_{\mathrm{meas}}}{\Gamma_{\mathrm{roof}}} = \frac{\class{mj-td}{\eta_{TD}}}{\class{mj-ar}{\eta_{AR}}}. \]

In particular, the bound underestimates the measured gain exactly when TD runs closer to its roofline than AR, and in general it bounds the measured gain in neither direction. As in Part 0, "bound" means the roofline bound \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{roof}}\), a ratio of two lower bounds on time, not a bound on \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{meas}}\).

Proof

The tokens per step cancel: \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{meas}}/\Gamma_{\mathrm{roof}} = (\class{mj-td}{\tau_{TD}}/\class{mj-td}{t_{TD}})\,/\,(\class{mj-ar}{\tau_{AR}}/\class{mj-ar}{t_{AR}})\). \(\blacksquare\)

Figure 43 · interactive

The bound is conservative while TD runs closer to its roofline than AR, up to batch 8, and optimistic from batch 16 on.

Choose a context; hover over or tap a batch to read the two efficiencies and their ratio.

Step efficiency \(\eta_X = \tau_X/t_X\) of each decoder, its empirical roofline time over its measured step time, medians of three repeats. By Proposition 9 the measured gain over the bound is \(\class{mj-td}{\eta_{TD}}/\class{mj-ar}{\eta_{AR}}\): the band between the curves is orange where the measured gain exceeds the bound and blue where it falls short. From batch 1 to the largest measured batch, AR's efficiency rises from 0.27–0.32 to 0.62–0.69, while TD's stays between 0.42 and 0.61. The batch axis is logarithmic: the measured sizes 1, 2, 4, …, 64 are equally spaced.

The ratio is 1.22–1.88 up to batch 4, 1.02–1.07 at batch 8 and 0.80–0.94 from batch 16 on. AR's step efficiency rises faster with the batch than TD's, from 0.27–0.32 at batch 1 to 0.62–0.69 at batch 64, against 0.42–0.47 and 0.51 for TD: AR's latency-bound small GEMMs, idle time and time outside the model weigh less as its batch grows, while TD's batch is already large in tokens at batch 1. At batch 8 the bound and the measured gain agree within 8%, and from batch 16 on the bound exceeds the measurement by 6–24%. These ratios near 1 say that the two decoders run at similar fractions of their rooflines, about half, not that either is close to its roofline.

What the roofline gets right, and what it needs

  • The shape holds, from batch 1. The measured gain falls with the batch at every context: 7.0 at batch 1 and context 1k, 1.04 at batch 32, and AR is faster from somewhere between batch 32 and 64 at contexts 1k–4k. Bound (a) of Part 8, with datasheet rates and independent routing (A5), first rises, up to batch 4–8 at contexts 1k–16k, as Part 3 predicts; at the measured routing it falls from batch 1, like the measurement. Against the context the measured gain falls slowly, from 1.57 at batch 16 and 1k to 1.22 at 64k. The technical report's 7.1 at batch 1 on an H100 and its crossover near 32 requests are close to these, with another accelerator, prompt length and sampler.
  • Routing moves the bound most, in both directions. Assumption (A5) fails for both decoders. Uneven expert popularity and the dependence between the positions of a canvas lower the linear penalty at batch 1 from 7.9 to 4.3; Proposition 1 then gives 4.3 against 2.3 under (A5), and the exact accounting 4.2 against 2.7; the measured gain is 7.0. At large batch the same popularity makes AR cheaper still, which moves the parity batch from the Summary's estimate near 118 (BF16, independent routing (A5), prompt 1,024 and 8,192 tokens generated) to between 32 and 64 here, at contexts 1k–4k. The book's headline numbers are bounds under (A5); the measured ones should be read alongside them.
  • Measured ceilings matter where one decoder is compute-bound. The power cap lowers compute more than bandwidth, so the roofline bound loses up to a quarter where TD is compute-bound and AR is not.
  • The ratio depends on equal tuning. By Proposition 9, any kernel that helps one decoder more than the other moves the measured gain by the same factor. TD received two custom kernels and AR none; tuning AR's small GEMMs, idle time and time outside the model would lower the measured gain at small batch, where it now exceeds the bound.

Limitations

  • One accelerator and one pair of models. The measurements use one H200, DiffusionGemma, and Gemma 4 26B-A4B as its AR counterpart, rather than an AR decoder with DiffusionGemma's own weights.
  • One workload. All prompts ask for long essays about PG-19 passages, in each model's chat template; AR samples at temperature 1 and TD with its own temperature schedule, with a fixed \(S = 14\) and every canvas position committed together. Quality is checked on GSM8K and IFEval only. With this fixed schedule TD's answers degrade at long context: 58–88% of its measured canvases are text-like (at least 40 distinct tokens of 256) at context 1k, 15–31% at 64k from batch 2 on and none at batch 1 and 64k, against 98–100% of AR's measured windows. Routing, and hence the gain, may differ on other text; the 64k results, above all at batch 1, are the least representative.
  • Work the roofline does not count. The engine evaluates the vocabulary head in the commit pass of every canvas and the soft embedding in its first denoising pass; the roofline counts neither, since their outputs are not used. Their time therefore appears as inefficiency of the head component, whose efficiency could not exceed about 0.93 even with ideal kernels.
  • Precision. The measurements use FP8 weights; the headline numbers of Parts 1–7 are BF16.
  • Throughput only. All requests of a point share one prompt length but not one position, since requests that start decoding early run up to four canvases ahead; prefill, the time to the first canvas and per-request latency are not measured.
  • Variance. Three repeats per point, and one for the stock-kernel reference of Part 10. At batch 1 the experts a canvas touches vary most between repeats, from 38 to 76 per layer at context 1k, so batch-1 results are the least precise.

Code and data

Every measurement of Parts 8–11 comes from the harness roofscope, and every code excerpt in these chapters quotes it at one commit. The pipeline below goes from the runs on the GPU to the numbers in the figures.

Related work

  • Diffusion against autoregressive decoding. The DiffusionGemma technical report (2026) measures this model against Gemma 4 on an H100 in FP8 (Part 0); its gain is the tokens per forward pass divided by a per-step slowdown, the measured counterpart of Proposition 1, and it counts the experts a canvas touches. Asaria et al. (2026) study how DiffusionGemma commits tokens. Kim et al. (2025) combine a roofline analysis with profiling of LLaDA-8B against LLaMA-3-8B: AR models batch better, and block-wise decoding makes arithmetic intensity independent of the generation length. Peng et al. (2025) find AR faster than open diffusion models in most settings, with the gains of caching and parallel decoding confined to small batches. dInfer measures an MoE diffusion model in a serving engine. The book adds a closed form of the bound over batch, context, canvas and accelerator, the expert and selection penalties, sparse attention, and an attribution of the measured gap to kernels.
  • Speculative decoding, the other way to commit several tokens per pass (Leviathan et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023), has the same accounting: verifying a draft is a pass over several positions. MoESD (2025) models the experts touched with the same \(U_{E,k}(N)\) under uniform independent routing and finds it close to its measured counts; Part 8 shows that a canvas departs from it. MagicDec finds speculative decoding effective at large batch once the KV cache dominates, the counterpart of Part 4's regime.
  • Parallel decoding with adaptive commits. Fast-dLLM commits positions whose confidence clears a threshold and caches keys and values approximately; dInfer builds an inference framework on such methods. Both make the tokens per forward pass, fixed at 17.1 here, a variable traded against quality.
  • Routing locality. The Mixtral report finds consecutive tokens repeating experts more often than chance in its upper layers, and Liang et al. (2025) measure local routing consistency across 20 MoE models. For MoE diffusion models, Wei et al. (2026) report consistent routing across the positions and steps of a block and use it to skip experts, and Feng et al. (2026) report that block decoding raises the count of distinct experts until MoE inference is memory-bound, and train block-level experts that lower it. Part 8 measures the size of this dependence for DiffusionGemma and its effect on the bound.
  • Rooflines, power and inference cost. The roofline model is due to Williams, Waterman and Patterson (2009), and its empirical ceilings to the Empirical Roofline Toolkit (Lo et al., "Roofline model toolkit: a practical tool for architectural and program analysis", PMBS 2014). Choi et al. extend it to energy ("A roofline model of energy", IPDPS 2013); Patel et al. (2024) characterise power capping for LLM inference, and Luo et al. (2025) microbenchmark Hopper. Pope et al. (2022) and Austin et al. (2025) give the standard accounting of transformer inference cost.
  • Kernels. The kernels of Part 10 build on vLLM and PagedAttention (Kwon et al., 2023), FlashAttention 3 and FlashAttention 4, grouped MoE GEMMs such as MegaBlocks and DeepGEMM, and SonicMoE, which also fuses the gather, activation and reduction around the expert GEMMs. FlashMLA's kernel write-up handles a 512-dimensional value head by splitting the output between two warpgroups of one CTA and reaches 660 TFLOP/s on an H800; it also reports the clock throttling under load that Part 8 measures. It was not compared here.

Open problems

  • A grouped expert GEMM of cuBLAS quality, with producer and consumer warps and the fused epilogues of Part 10: the largest recoverable time of TD at batch 2–8.
  • Global attention at batch 1, where calls stay on FlashAttention 4 at about half of the attention ceiling; splitting the keys across more CTAs would fill the GPU.
  • An exchange that overlaps compute in the pair kernel, which now waits for the partner's scores before each softmax.
  • Time outside the model, the first recoverable time from batch 16 on: it should be split into named kernels before anything is fused.
  • Equal tuning of AR, so that Proposition 9 compares like with like.
  • Routing per sequence and per position, to separate the dependence between the positions of a canvas from expert popularity that differs between sequences, which the run-level frequencies \(\rho_e\) of Part 8 pool.
  • Measurement with the adaptive sampler, which keeps long answers coherent but varies the passes per canvas, so that \(\omega\) becomes a measured quantity rather than a fixed 15.
  • A model of \(N^{\mathrm{eff}}\) in terms of the batch, the context and the step of the denoising schedule, which would let Parts 3–5 use measured routing in closed form.
